name: Helios
license: MPL 2.0 (Helios build tooling); the illumos core is mostly CDDL
summary: Oxide’s distribution of illumos, the operating system on every sled’s host CPU in the Oxide rack, where it runs VMs on its bhyve hypervisor and the control plane in zones.
intro: Helios is the host operating system of the Oxide rack: the illumos kernel and userland, built from Oxide’s `stlouis` branch of illumos-gate. Its README calls the packages “mostly stock illumos” with additions for Oxide hardware. The Helios repository holds the tools that build it from several consolidations: the OS itself, build scripts for packages beyond the core OS, a zone brand for Omicron components, and boot tools.

On a sled it boots without a UEFI BIOS. The AMD platform security processor loads Oxide’s tiny `phbl` loader from flash, which switches the CPU into 64-bit mode, unpacks a compressed boot archive and jumps to the illumos kernel. The OS that Omicron installs on a sled is a whole image: a 32 MiB boot ROM plus a root file system ramdisk.

Once up, Helios provides what the rest of the rack is built on: bhyve as the kernel half of the hypervisor (Propolis is the user-space half), zones to isolate each control plane service and each VM’s monitor, ZFS on the sleds’ SSDs, SMF to supervise services, the Fault Management Architecture, and DTrace and core files for debugging in the field. OPTE’s virtual networking runs inside it as a kernel module.
strengths: Isolation primitives built in: each service and each VM’s Propolis runs in its own zone with its own network stack
Debugging tools Oxide wanted in production: DTrace for live tracing, rich core files for postmortem analysis and FMA for hardware faults
A small, controlled boot path with no UEFI firmware stack, and the OS delivered as one image
Open source, including the kernel branch and the build tooling, so customers can read the OS their rack runs
limits: It is built for Oxide hardware and x86 only; on a laptop it runs as a VM for development, not on Arm Macs
Not every consolidation is public: AMD CPU firmware, Chelsio T6 NIC firmware and some low-level tools are listed as “will be available in future”
illumos has a much smaller community than Linux, so Oxide takes on more of the maintenance itself
Customers never run it directly: it is the rack’s host OS, and guests bring their own operating systems

snippet.title: Build illumos the Helios way and install it as a new boot environment (on a Helios machine, from the README)
source: gmake setup                         # builds ./helios-build and clones illumos (stlouis)
./helios-build onu -t my-be-name    # install into boot environment my-be-name

story: The Oxide rack’s host CPU had to run customer VMs, distributed storage and the control plane, so the choice of operating system and hypervisor came together. RFD 26, by Joshua M. Clulow, Patrick Mooney and Robert Mustacchi, compared KVM on Linux with bhyve on illumos. Beyond the hypervisor, it weighed what a small team supporting critical infrastructure would need: service supervision, isolation, fault management, and the ability to debug a defect fully from its first occurrence, with DTrace and postmortem core files. It also noted that illumos raised no objection to kernel modules written outside the core tree or in Rust.

By June 2021, after reducing the risk of building on illumos and working with the Rust community on illumos toolchain issues, Oxide decided on Helios, its illumos distribution, as the host OS, with bhyve and Propolis for guests. Its May 2021 milestone demo had already run Helios on an AMD EPYC 7402P system with Omicron, CockroachDB and ClickHouse on top. The same reasoning led Oxide to drop the UEFI stack in favor of its own boot path.
Helios shipped in the first racks in 2023 and was open-sourced in January 2024, prompting an Oxide and Friends episode on its history. Its packages remain mostly stock illumos.

choices.why: RFD 26 valued illumos’s zones, SMF, FMA, DTrace and postmortem debugging for a small team that must fix defects from few incidents, and its stable kernel interfaces and openness to modules in Rust.

choices.choice: No UEFI firmware on the host
choices.why: Oxide intended to discard the UEFI stack for host bootstrap in favor of something that met its needs more directly; `phbl` loads the OS straight from flash.

timeline.text: Runs on an AMD EPYC 7402P at Oxide’s May milestone demo; RFD 26 picks Helios as the host OS (June)
Ships as the host OS of the first Oxide racks
